Deep Learning for Species Distribution Modelling

DeepMaxEnt — from occurrence data to calibrated habitat maps

Learning objectives

After completing this module you should be able to:

  1. Explain why maximum entropy is a principled default for species distribution modelling from presence-only data.
  2. Describe how the MaxEnt objective can be embedded in a neural network loss function to extend classical MaxEnt to non-linear feature interactions.
  3. Load and filter GBIF occurrence records and pair them with CHELSA-BIOCLIM+ bioclimatic rasters using rasterio.
  4. Construct presence/background training tensors and run a DeepMaxEnt training loop in PyTorch.
  5. Interpret a predicted suitability map and reason about its uncertainty in regions with sparse occurrence records.
Note

This page presents a simplified walkthrough of the tutorial notebook available at github.com/RYCKEWAERT/deepmaxent.

Reference: Ryckewaert M. et al. (2026). Applying the maximum entropy principle to neural networks enhances multi-species distribution models. Methods in Ecology and Evolution. https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210x.70262

Background: why MaxEnt for SDMs?

The presence-only problem

Field surveys rarely confirm absences. A species not recorded at a location may be absent, or it may simply not have been detected. Species distribution models (SDMs) are therefore typically trained on presence-only data: a set of confirmed occurrence locations \(\{x_1, \ldots, x_n\} \subset \mathcal{X}\), where \(\mathcal{X}\) is the environmental space of the study region.

The challenge is to infer a probability distribution \(\hat{p}(x)\) — the predicted occurrence probability — from presences alone, without a confirmed absence class.

The MaxEnt principle

The classical solution (Phillips et al., 2006) applies the maximum entropy principle: among all distributions consistent with the observed data, choose the one with maximum entropy — i.e. the least informative one given the evidence. Formally, MaxEnt finds \(\hat{p}\) that solves:

\[\hat{p} = \arg\max_{p} H(p) \quad \text{subject to} \quad \mathbb{E}_{p}[f_k(x)] = \mathbb{E}_{\text{occ}}[f_k(x)], \quad k = 1, \ldots, K\]

where \(H(p) = -\sum_x p(x) \log p(x)\) is entropy, \(f_k\) are feature functions of the environment (temperature, precipitation, …), and the constraints enforce that the model’s expected feature values match those observed at occurrence locations.

The solution takes a Gibbs distribution form:

\[\hat{p}(x) \propto \exp\!\left(\sum_k \lambda_k f_k(x)\right)\]

where \(\lambda_k\) are Lagrange multipliers, equivalent to the weights of a log-linear model.

From linear features to neural networks

Classical MaxEnt is restricted to hand-crafted, fixed feature functions (linear, quadratic, product terms). DeepMaxEnt replaces this fixed feature map with a shared neural network \(g_\theta : \mathbb{R}^P \to \mathbb{R}^C\), which learns a common latent environmental representation across all modelled species jointly. The occurrence intensity of species \(j\) at site \(i\) is obtained by combining the shared network output with species-specific parameters \(\alpha_j\):

\[\lambda_{ij} = \exp\!\left(\alpha_j^\top\, g_\theta(x_i)\right)\]

The DeepMaxEnt loss is defined as a weighted sum of species-wise cross-entropy losses, with intensities normalised across all \(K\) sites for each species independently:

\[\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}, \mathbf{Y}) = -\frac{1}{KN} \sum_{j=1}^{N} \sum_{i=1}^{K} y_{ij} \log\!\left(\frac{\lambda_{ij}}{\sum_{k=1}^{K} \lambda_{kj}}\right)\]

where \(y_{ij}\) is the observed presence of species \(j\) at site \(i\), \(\lambda_{ij}\) the predicted intensity, \(K\) the number of sites (background + presence), and \(N\) the number of species. Equivalently, at the parameter level:

\[\mathcal{L}(\theta, \alpha) = -\sum_j \left[ \frac{1}{n_j} \sum_{i \in \text{occ}_j} \log \lambda_{ij} - \log \sum_{x \in \mathcal{B}} \lambda_{jx} \right]\]

This per-species normalisation decouples parameter updates from absolute occurrence counts, distinguishing DeepMaxEnt from a standard Poisson loss in the multi-species setting: a species with 5 occurrences and one with 500 contribute equally to the gradient, preventing high-frequency species from dominating training.

Data: Costa Rica plant occurrences (GBIF)

The tutorial uses plant occurrence records from GBIF for Costa Rica — a high-biodiversity country with dense sampling coverage, making it suitable for a methodological demonstration.

Environmental predictors are the CHELSA-BIOCLIM+ global climate layers (Brun et al., 2022), a kilometre-resolution dataset of bioclimatic variables capturing temperature and precipitation seasonality.

Step 1 — Import libraries

import sys, os, warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

# DeepMaxEnt library lives alongside the data
sys.path.insert(0, 'data/deepmaxent')

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from tqdm import tqdm

import rasterio
import rasterio.transform

import torch
import torch.optim as optim
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import plotly.graph_objects as go

from librairies.model import deepmaxent_model
from librairies.losses import deepmaxent_loss
from librairies.utils import set_seed

NAVY = '#1b3a5c'
TEAL = '#2a7f7f'

set_seed(42)
print("Libraries loaded.")
Libraries loaded.

Step 2 — Load and filter occurrence records

df = pd.read_csv('data/deepmaxent/biodiversity_data.csv', sep='\t', low_memory=False)

print(f"Raw observations: {df.shape[0]:,} × {df.shape[1]} columns")

df['decimalLatitude']  = pd.to_numeric(df['decimalLatitude'],  errors='coerce')
df['decimalLongitude'] = pd.to_numeric(df['decimalLongitude'], errors='coerce')
df_clean = df.dropna(subset=['decimalLatitude', 'decimalLongitude', 'species'])

df_plants = df_clean[
    (df_clean['kingdom'] == 'Plantae') &
    (df_clean['basisOfRecord'] == 'HUMAN_OBSERVATION')
].copy()

print(f"Plant observations (human): {len(df_plants):,}")
print(f"Unique species: {df_plants['species'].nunique():,}")
print(f"Longitude range: [{df_plants['decimalLongitude'].min():.2f}, "
      f"{df_plants['decimalLongitude'].max():.2f}]")
print(f"Latitude range:  [{df_plants['decimalLatitude'].min():.2f}, "
      f"{df_plants['decimalLatitude'].max():.2f}]")
Raw observations: 26,670 × 50 columns
Plant observations (human): 1,145
Unique species: 102
Longitude range: [-85.92, -82.63]
Latitude range:  [8.23, 11.19]

Why filter to human observations? Machine-recorded occurrences (e.g. automatic traps, preserved specimens without precise geolocation) have heterogeneous spatial accuracy. Human observations submitted through platforms such as iNaturalist carry standardised GPS coordinates and are therefore more suitable as training points for spatially explicit models.

fig = go.Figure(go.Scattergeo(

fig.update_geos(

Step 4 — Load pre-cropped environmental rasters

The CHELSA-BIOCLIM+ rasters are already cropped to the study region extent. Each .tif file contains one bioclimatic variable at ~1 km resolution.

raster_dir = 'data/deepmaxent/cropped_rasters/'
raster_files = sorted([f for f in os.listdir(raster_dir) if f.endswith('.tif')])

env_bands = []
transform_ref, crs_ref = None, None
lon_min = lon_max = lat_min = lat_max = None

for fname in tqdm(raster_files, desc='Loading rasters'):
    with rasterio.open(os.path.join(raster_dir, fname)) as src:
        band = src.read(1).astype(float)
        if src.nodata is not None:
            band[band == src.nodata] = np.nan
        env_bands.append(band)
        if transform_ref is None:
            transform_ref = src.transform
            crs_ref       = src.crs
            lon_min, lat_min, lon_max, lat_max = src.bounds

env_stack = np.stack(env_bands, axis=0)   # (n_vars, height, width)
print(f"Environmental stack: {env_stack.shape}  "
      f"({env_stack.shape[0]} variables, {env_stack.shape[1]}×{env_stack.shape[2]} pixels)")
print(f"Extent: lon [{lon_min:.3f}, {lon_max:.3f}]  lat [{lat_min:.3f}, {lat_max:.3f}]")
Environmental stack: (19, 378, 418)  (19 variables, 378×418 pixels)
Extent: lon [-86.017, -82.534]  lat [8.139, 11.289]

Step 5 — Prepare multi-species training tensors

In single-species MaxEnt, background points are random samples from the study region that approximate the environmental space available to the species. In multi-species DeepMaxEnt this step is unnecessary: the occurrence locations of all other species in the dataset already represent the accessible environmental space. A site where species B was observed is — by definition — reachable and environmentally sampled, making it a valid background point for species A. The softmax normalisation in the loss function automatically treats all sites in the dataset as the denominator for each species independently.

This means the training set is simply the union of all species’ presence pixels, with a multi-hot label matrix \(\mathbf{Y} \in \{0,1\}^{K \times N}\) where \(Y_{ij} = 1\) if species \(j\) has at least one confirmed observation in pixel \(i\).

n_vars, height, width = env_stack.shape

# Keep species with a minimum number of observations; cap for tutorial speed
min_obs    = 20
max_species = 100
species_counts = df_plants.groupby('species').size()
valid_species  = (species_counts[species_counts >= min_obs]
                  .nlargest(max_species).index.tolist())
n_species      = len(valid_species)
species_to_idx = {sp: i for i, sp in enumerate(valid_species)}
print(f"Modelling {n_species} plant species (≥{min_obs} observations each)")

# Rasterise each species independently
species_pixels = {}
for sp in valid_species:
    sp_df = df_plants[df_plants['species'] == sp]
    r_sp, c_sp = rasterio.transform.rowcol(
        transform_ref,
        sp_df['decimalLongitude'].values,
        sp_df['decimalLatitude'].values,
    )
    r_sp, c_sp = np.asarray(r_sp), np.asarray(c_sp)
    ok = (r_sp >= 0) & (r_sp < height) & (c_sp >= 0) & (c_sp < width)
    species_pixels[sp] = set(zip(r_sp[ok].tolist(), c_sp[ok].tolist()))

# Union of all presence pixels = training sites
all_pres_set  = set().union(*species_pixels.values())
all_pres_list = list(all_pres_set)
pixel_to_idx  = {rc: k for k, rc in enumerate(all_pres_list)}
pres_rows = np.array([rc[0] for rc in all_pres_list])
pres_cols = np.array([rc[1] for rc in all_pres_list])
print(f"Training sites: {len(all_pres_list):,} unique pixels (union of all species)")

# Environmental values at training sites; remove any NaN pixels
X_pres   = env_stack[:, pres_rows, pres_cols].T          # (n_sites, n_vars)
nan_mask = np.any(np.isnan(X_pres), axis=1)
X_pres   = X_pres[~nan_mask]
clean_list   = [rc for rc, keep in zip(all_pres_list, (~nan_mask).tolist()) if keep]
clean_lookup = {rc: k for k, rc in enumerate(clean_list)}
n_sites  = len(clean_list)

# Multi-hot label matrix  Y[site, species] = 1 iff species observed at that pixel
Y_labels = np.zeros((n_sites, n_species), dtype=np.float32)
for sp, sp_idx in species_to_idx.items():
    for rc in species_pixels[sp]:
        k = clean_lookup.get(rc)
        if k is not None:
            Y_labels[k, sp_idx] = 1.0

# Standardise features on a broad environmental sample (not just presences)
valid_mask_all = ~np.any(np.isnan(env_stack), axis=0)
valid_rows_all, valid_cols_all = np.where(valid_mask_all)
rng       = np.random.default_rng(42)
sc_idx    = rng.choice(len(valid_rows_all), size=min(20_000, len(valid_rows_all)), replace=False)
X_scaler  = env_stack[:, valid_rows_all[sc_idx], valid_cols_all[sc_idx]].T
scaler    = StandardScaler().fit(X_scaler)

X_pres_s = scaler.transform(X_pres)
X_pres_t = torch.tensor(X_pres_s, dtype=torch.float32)
Y_labels_t = torch.tensor(Y_labels, dtype=torch.float32)

print(f"Label matrix: {Y_labels.shape}  "
      f"(mean presences per site: {Y_labels.sum(1).mean():.2f})")
Modelling 10 plant species (≥20 observations each)
Training sites: 580 unique pixels (union of all species)
Label matrix: (580, 10)  (mean presences per site: 1.06)

Step 6 — Build and train the DeepMaxEnt model

The DeepMaxEnt architecture consists of a shared neural network backbone \(g_\theta : \mathbb{R}^P \to \mathbb{R}^C\) followed by \(N\) species-specific linear heads \(\alpha_j \in \mathbb{R}^C\). The predicted intensity of species \(j\) at site \(i\) is \(\lambda_{ij} = \exp(\alpha_j^\top g_\theta(x_i))\).

Training minimises the species-wise normalised cross-entropy:

\[\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\Lambda}, \mathbf{Y}) = -\frac{1}{KN} \sum_{j=1}^{N} \sum_{i=1}^{K} y_{ij} \log\!\left(\frac{\lambda_{ij}}{\sum_{k=1}^{K} \lambda_{kj}}\right)\]

Normalising across sites for each species independently ensures that rare and common species contribute equally to gradient updates.

n_features = X_pres_t.shape[1]
model     = deepmaxent_model(input_size=n_features, hidden_size=128,
                             output_size=n_species, hidden_nbr=3)
criterion = deepmaxent_loss()

optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=1e-4)
scheduler = optim.lr_scheduler.StepLR(optimizer, step_size=50, gamma=0.5)

n_epochs = 150
losses   = []

for epoch in range(n_epochs):
    model.train()
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss = criterion(model(X_pres_t), Y_labels_t)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
    scheduler.step()
    losses.append(loss.item())
    if (epoch + 1) % 30 == 0:
        print(f"Epoch {epoch+1:3d}/{n_epochs}  loss = {loss.item():.4f}")
Epoch  30/150  loss = 0.6097
Epoch  60/150  loss = 0.5943
Epoch  90/150  loss = 0.5861
Epoch 120/150  loss = 0.5807
Epoch 150/150  loss = 0.5769
fig = go.Figure(go.Scatter(
    x=list(range(1, len(losses) + 1)), y=losses,
    mode='lines', line=dict(color=NAVY, width=2), name='Training loss'
))
for ep, label in [(50, 'LR ×0.5'), (100, 'LR ×0.5')]:
    fig.add_vline(x=ep, line_dash='dash', line_color=TEAL, line_width=1.4,
                  annotation_text=label, annotation_position='top right',
                  annotation_font_size=11)
fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title='Epoch', yaxis_title='DeepMaxEnt loss',
    title='Training convergence — DeepMaxEnt',
    template='simple_white', height=340
)
fig.show()

Step 7 — Evaluate per-species AUC and select focal species

from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    train_preds = model(X_pres_t).numpy()   # (n_sites, n_species)

auc_dict = {}
for sp, sp_idx in species_to_idx.items():
    y_true = Y_labels[:, sp_idx]
    if y_true.sum() < 5 or (1 - y_true).sum() < 5:
        continue
    try:
        auc_dict[sp] = roc_auc_score(y_true, train_preds[:, sp_idx])
    except Exception:
        pass

auc_sorted = sorted(auc_dict.items(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
print("Top 5 species by AUC (evaluated on training sites):")
for sp, auc_val in auc_sorted[:5]:
    n_pres = int(Y_labels[:, species_to_idx[sp]].sum())
    print(f"  {sp:<40}  AUC = {auc_val:.3f}  (n = {n_pres})")

top_species = [sp for sp, _ in auc_sorted[:2]]
Top 5 species by AUC (evaluated on training sites):
  Puya dasylirioides                        AUC = 0.964  (n = 103)
  Gunnera talamancana                       AUC = 0.961  (n = 25)
  Tectona grandis                           AUC = 0.949  (n = 65)
  Peperomia rotundifolia                    AUC = 0.941  (n = 29)
  Cedrela odorata                           AUC = 0.907  (n = 21)

Step 8 — Predict and map habitat suitability

Predictions are computed on all valid (non-NaN) pixels of the study region. To keep memory usage reasonable the model output is extracted only for the two focal species; the suitability is then mapped with full geographic context using Plotly’s geo layout (ocean, coastlines, country borders).

top_indices = [species_to_idx[sp] for sp in top_species]

# Predict over the full grid in batches
valid_env = env_stack[:, valid_rows_all, valid_cols_all].T
X_full_s  = scaler.transform(valid_env)
X_full_t  = torch.tensor(X_full_s, dtype=torch.float32)

batch_size  = 20_000
logit_parts = []
model.eval()
for i in range(0, len(X_full_t), batch_size):
    with torch.no_grad():
        batch = model(X_full_t[i:i+batch_size]).numpy()
    logit_parts.append(batch[:, top_indices])

full_logits = np.vstack(logit_parts)          # (n_valid, 2)
full_suit   = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-full_logits))  # sigmoid → [0, 1]

# Build 1-D geographic axes (shared across both species maps)
lon_coords = np.array([transform_ref.c + (j + 0.5) * transform_ref.a for j in range(width)])
lat_coords = np.array([transform_ref.f + (i + 0.5) * transform_ref.e for i in range(height)])

print(f"Grid: {len(valid_rows_all):,} valid pixels  |  Focal species: {top_species}")
Grid: 158,004 valid pixels  |  Focal species: ['Puya dasylirioides', 'Gunnera talamancana']
sp      = top_species[0]
auc_val = auc_dict.get(sp, float('nan'))
n_pres  = int(Y_labels[:, species_to_idx[sp]].sum())

suit_grid_sp1 = np.full((height, width), np.nan)
suit_grid_sp1[valid_rows_all, valid_cols_all] = full_suit[:, 0]

fig = go.Figure(go.Heatmap(
    z=suit_grid_sp1,
    x=lon_coords, y=lat_coords,
    colorscale='YlGn', zmin=0, zmax=1,
    colorbar=dict(title='Suitability', thickness=14, len=0.85),
    hovertemplate='Lon: %{x:.3f}°<br>Lat: %{y:.3f}°<br>Suitability: %{z:.3f}<extra></extra>',
))
fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title='Longitude (°)', yaxis_title='Latitude (°)',
    title=f'<i>{sp}</i> — suitability  (AUC = {auc_val:.3f}, n = {n_pres})',
    template='simple_white', height=500,
    yaxis=dict(scaleanchor='x', scaleratio=1),
)
fig.show()
sp      = top_species[1]
auc_val = auc_dict.get(sp, float('nan'))
n_pres  = int(Y_labels[:, species_to_idx[sp]].sum())

suit_grid_sp2 = np.full((height, width), np.nan)
suit_grid_sp2[valid_rows_all, valid_cols_all] = full_suit[:, 1]

fig = go.Figure(go.Heatmap(
    z=suit_grid_sp2,
    x=lon_coords, y=lat_coords,
    colorscale='YlGn', zmin=0, zmax=1,
    colorbar=dict(title='Suitability', thickness=14, len=0.85),
    hovertemplate='Lon: %{x:.3f}°<br>Lat: %{y:.3f}°<br>Suitability: %{z:.3f}<extra></extra>',
))
fig.update_layout(
    xaxis_title='Longitude (°)', yaxis_title='Latitude (°)',
    title=f'<i>{sp}</i> — suitability  (AUC = {auc_val:.3f}, n = {n_pres})',
    template='simple_white', height=500,
    yaxis=dict(scaleanchor='x', scaleratio=1),
)
fig.show()

Interpretation notes

The predicted suitability maps should be read with the following caveats in mind:

  1. The multi-species background. In multi-species DeepMaxEnt no random background points are added. Instead, the presence locations of all other species in the dataset serve as the implicit background for each species through the softmax normalisation in the loss. This is ecologically sound because co-occurring species share the same accessible environmental space.

  2. Suitability is not probability of occurrence. The model predicts relative environmental suitability, not detectability-adjusted occupancy probability. High suitability in a pixel does not mean the species is present — it means the environment is consistent with observed presences.

  3. Extrapolation beyond training conditions. In pixels whose environmental values fall outside the range of training data, the network extrapolates. MaxEnt’s entropy constraint makes this extrapolation conservative by default, but it is not guaranteed to be ecologically meaningful.

  4. AUC on training sites. The AUC values reported in Step 7 are computed on the training pixels themselves (presence vs. background sites within the training set). They are useful for ranking species but should not be confused with proper out-of-sample validation metrics.

References

  • Brun, P., Zimmermann, N. E., Hari, C., Pellissier, L., & Karger, D. N. (2022). CHELSA-BIOCLIM+ A novel set of global climate-related predictors at kilometre-resolution. EnviDat. https://www.doi.org/10.16904/envidat.332
  • Phillips, S. J., Anderson, R. P., & Schapire, R. E. (2006). Maximum entropy modeling of species geographic distributions. Ecological Modelling, 190(3–4), 231–259. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2005.03.026
  • Renner, I. W., & Warton, D. I. (2013). Equivalence of MAXENT and Poisson point process models for species distribution modeling in ecology. Biometrics, 69(1), 274–281. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1541-0420.2012.01824.x
  • Ryckewaert M. et al. (2026). Applying the maximum entropy principle to neural networks enhances multi-species distribution models. Methods in Ecology and Evolution. https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210x.70262
